stories.title: AWS puts sandbox tasks inside durable workflows
stories.summary: An AWS developer preview lets Lambda durable functions manage MicroVM sessions, checkpoint work and retry failed tasks.
stories.topic: Isolated code execution and workflow recovery
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: A build service runs generated code in an isolated VM, keeping working files together for related steps and recording progress in the calling workflow.

facts.text: On November 25, AWS announced a developer preview for orchestrating Lambda MicroVMs with durable functions in TypeScript and Python.
The extension supports individual tasks and sessions whose tasks share memory and files.
AWS says the durable function manages the VM lifecycle, checkpoints progress and retries failed tasks.
AWS advises against production use during the developer preview.

stories.changed: Lambda MicroVMs already provided isolated execution. The extension adds lifecycle and task management to the durable function that calls them.
stories.whyItMatters: Running generated code in a VM is one part of the job. Teams also need to recover interrupted work and know which steps ran. The preview puts those concerns in one workflow.
stories.technicalImpact: Separate unrelated jobs into different sessions. Review what state persists between tasks. Test how retries behave after partial writes or other external side effects.
stories.businessImpact: Teams may spend less time maintaining a custom sandbox scheduler. Existing worker systems may still offer better portability or established controls.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if the extension reaches general availability with predictable recovery behavior and costs, it could make isolated execution easier to include in long-running build workflows.
uncertainties: AWS provides no comparative cost, latency or recovery data for the preview.
A workflow checkpoint does not undo an external write. The application still needs to guard against duplicate effects.
State shared within a session needs an explicit lifetime and ownership boundary.
stories.analysis: Starting an isolated VM is only the first step. AWS has made the job's progress and the life of its sandbox part of the same workflow. The preview gives teams a way to see how that holds up when a job fails halfway through.

stories.title: Google Workspace sets a deadline for agent access
stories.summary: Google is rolling out managed access for Workspace agents and says it will start enforcing its MCP requirement on February 1, 2027. Teams that built agents on direct REST calls now have a migration to plan.
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: An internal agent reads Drive files using the same OAuth client as a conventional integration. Its team inventories both paths and tests an agent-specific client against the managed Workspace tools before enforcement begins.

facts.text: Google announced general availability for its Workspace MCP servers and official CLI on November 24, with a two-week rollout.

Google says it will begin technical enforcement of the MCP requirement for agentic Workspace access on February 1, 2027. Its developer guidance calls for separate OAuth clients for traditional features and agentic access.

Google describes administrator controls for agent access, confirmation rules for sensitive actions, and audit records for agent actions and confirmations. Existing user-level data loss prevention policies also apply.

The addendum limits retention of defined Google Technical Information to 30 days, prohibits retaining it or covered user data after disconnection or revocation, and prohibits using those data for model training or building evaluation datasets.

stories.changed: The managed interfaces are rolling out with a published deadline to move covered agent access away from direct Workspace REST calls. The announcement gives developers both an integration target and a date to plan around.
stories.whyItMatters: An approved OAuth flow can become two different integration paths once an app adds an agent. Teams have to know which calls are agent-driven, which controls apply, and what cached data needs to disappear when access is revoked.
stories.technicalImpact: Inventory Workspace connectors and shared OAuth clients. Check tool coverage and permissions for each workflow, test how approvals and audit logs behave under the organization's policies, and verify deletion after disconnection.
stories.businessImpact: Teams with existing agents may need migration and testing time. Shared admin controls may simplify review, while dependence on Google's tool coverage can constrain integrations that rely on specific REST operations.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if enforcement works as announced and managed tools cover the operations teams rely on, agent-specific connectors may become a standard item in Workspace access reviews.
uncertainties: The rollout gives no evidence yet of lower incident rates or how consistently policies behave across every tool and tenant.
Administrative visibility and confirmation prompts can help reviewers, but legitimate access can still be used for an unintended task. Test the application’s own permission and approval boundaries.
Teams with workflows that lack equivalent managed tools may need to revise or defer features.
stories.analysis: The migration date is the important part. An engineering team can turn it into a real inventory of integrations, permissions and retained data. The work is finding where automation starts to act like an agent and giving that path an owner.

stories.title: The safety review moved into the customer’s bucket.
stories.summary: Amazon Bedrock now exposes model-provider access programs as inspectable cloud state, while preview Anthropic safeguards connect retained prompts, automated monitoring, customer-controlled storage, and customer adjudication. The workflow is tangible; its detection quality and safety outcomes remain unpublished.
stories.topic: Cloud control planes for frontier-model access, evidence custody, and safety review
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: A regulated company requests access to a frontier model through its cloud control plane. Administrators approve enrollment with IAM and organization policy, retained prompts land in a customer bucket under a customer key, automated monitoring creates a case, and the customer records whether the event violated policy.

facts.text: AWS published the Bedrock Trusted Access announcement with an embedded timestamp of 24 November 2026 at 05:01:14 UTC, inside this edition's research window.
AWS says the Trusted Access Program API is generally available and can discover, request, approve, enroll, disable, and inspect model-provider programs at project, account, or organization scope.
The first two programs, Anthropic Enterprise Frontier Safeguards and Enterprise Data Controls, are public previews rather than generally available safeguards.

Under EFS, Bedrock writes prompts and completions to a customer S3 bucket encrypted with a customer KMS key; automated monitoring runs in AWS-operated accounts, potential risks become cases in the customer's bucket, and the customer records violation or no-violation decisions.
AWS says EDC uses AWS-managed storage and keys while retaining a customer-review boundary, but the preview documentation says EDC cases are not delivered during preview.
The preview documentation instructs participants to use test accounts and test traffic, excludes PII and PHI, and says enrollment disables zero data retention for covered accounts or projects.
AWS says EFS records normally arrive within minutes but writes may retry for up to 72 hours; loss of required S3 or KMS access can stop covered-model service after 24 hours.

The reviewed sources publish no false-positive or false-negative rates, calibration data, case volume, reviewer burden, response time, enforcement outcome, adoption measure, or evidence of reduced misuse.

stories.changed: A frontier-model provider's special access terms can now be represented as cloud state: eligibility, approval, enrollment scope, retention mode, storage destination, key policy, evidence path, and customer review response. The API is GA, but the first safeguard programs remain preview-bound and operationally incomplete.
stories.whyItMatters: Enterprise teams can integrate model-access conditions into IAM, organization policy, storage, key management, evidence retention, and audit workflows instead of treating them as private account-team exceptions. Customer custody of retained evidence is meaningful, but it does not expose or validate the monitoring logic that decides which cases appear.
stories.technicalImpact: Separate enrollment authority from model use, log enrollment changes, test S3 and KMS failure paths, monitor evidence-delivery lag, define retention and reviewer access, and preserve incident runbooks for missing or delayed cases. Treat EFS and EDC as previews: do not use regulated data, assume API stability, or rely on an incomplete case interface.
stories.businessImpact: A cloud-native contract can make exceptional frontier access easier to audit, but it creates new dependencies and costs around storage, keys, reviewers, data retention, and model availability. Joining changes the zero-data-retention posture, and a broken evidence destination can eventually affect service continuity.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if other providers and clouds expose comparable enrollment, evidence, storage, case, and audit contracts—and publish detection and review outcomes—trusted-access programs could become a recognizable governance layer. One vendor's preview implementation does not establish that standard or prove improved safety.
uncertainties: AWS and Anthropic are the sources for the product behavior; no independent evaluator has published detection-quality or customer-outcome evidence for this implementation.
Customers control retained-data location, keys, and adjudication under EFS, but automated monitoring runs in AWS-operated accounts and its detection logic is undisclosed.
EDC cases are not delivered during the preview, so the announced customer-review boundary is not yet an operationally complete case workflow.
The preview excludes regulated data, has no console, can change APIs and action names, and is limited to specified regions, models, and inference profiles.
No source reports false positives, false negatives, calibration, case volume, reviewer burden, response SLAs, escalation outcomes, adoption, or measured misuse reduction.
Disabling zero data retention and coupling model availability to S3 and KMS access can create privacy, resilience, and operational trade-offs.
stories.analysis: The safeguard is becoming a contract the customer can inspect. That is progress because evidence location, enrollment authority, and review ownership are architecture—not fine print. But a case in a bucket is still only the output of an undisclosed detector. Custody is not calibration.

stories.title: The agent endpoint entered the firewall inventory.
stories.summary: AWS now discovers LLM, MCP, and A2A endpoints across common entry points and offers protocol-aware WAF inspection with optional Bedrock Guardrails checks. AI-specific interfaces have entered ordinary inventory and firewall policy; discovery completeness and protection effectiveness remain unmeasured.
stories.topic: AI endpoint inventory and protocol-aware managed inspection
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: A platform team discovers an undocumented MCP server behind a load balancer. The endpoint enters the same inventory as ordinary APIs, WAF recognizes its protocol, malformed requests can be blocked, and selected prompts or responses can be sent to Guardrails for content checks.

facts.text: AWS published its API and AI Security announcement with an embedded timestamp of 23 November 2026 at 20:25:17 UTC, inside this edition's research window.
AWS says API Portal can discover LLM inference, Model Context Protocol, and Agent2Agent endpoints behind API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, and CloudFront across an AWS organization.
API Portal builds inventory from service configuration and live traffic, identifies AI endpoint types, and can flag shadow, zombie, and orphaned APIs.
The generally available AWS WAF AI Security managed rule group recognizes LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic and checks malformed MCP and A2A requests against supported protocol versions.
When content inspection is enabled, AWS WAF can call Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to assess requests or responses for prompt attacks, harmful content, or sensitive information.
AWS says additional WAF fees apply and Bedrock charges separately for content inspection; API Portal and AI Security have different regional availability.

The reviewed sources publish no endpoint-discovery completeness measure, protocol coverage benchmark, false-positive or false-negative rate, prompt-injection bypass result, added-latency measurement, customer deployment count, blocked incident, or production outcome.

stories.changed: Agent-facing interfaces have moved into the same inventory and perimeter tooling used for ordinary APIs. AWS now identifies MCP, A2A, and LLM endpoints as network-visible application surfaces and applies protocol recognition, deterministic conformance checks, and optional content inspection at the WAF layer.
stories.whyItMatters: MCP and A2A make tools and cooperating agents reachable through self-describing protocols that can appear outside a central API registry. Discovering those interfaces and attaching managed inspection reduces the chance that an experimental server remains invisible. It does not decide whether an allowed tool call is authorized in application context.
stories.technicalImpact: Inventory AI endpoints from configuration and traffic, assign ownership, retire zombie paths, validate protocol versions, authenticate callers, verify tokens or signatures, set request-size and rate controls, and test content inspection for latency and bypass behavior. Keep application authorization, transaction policy, and tool-level permissions behind the perimeter.
stories.businessImpact: Security teams gain a familiar operating surface for AI endpoints, but protection adds regional, cost, tuning, and incident-response work. Managed rules can accelerate coverage while also creating false-positive, latency, and concentration risks that require measurement before broad enforcement.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if independent testing shows reliable endpoint coverage, bounded latency, and credible bypass and false-positive rates, protocol-aware inventory and inspection could become standard agent-platform controls. Without that evidence, AWS has established a control surface—not its effectiveness.
uncertainties: AWS is the source for discovery and protection claims; no independent benchmark or customer outcome validates the launch.
No source quantifies endpoint-discovery completeness, classification accuracy, protocol coverage, false positives, false negatives, added latency, or prompt-injection bypass rates.
Managed protocol and content inspection cannot determine whether an otherwise valid tool call is authorized by current user intent, application state, or business policy.
Response inspection is optional and limited by the body size AWS WAF inspects for the protected resource, leaving content beyond that limit unchecked.
Different regional availability and separate WAF and Bedrock charges can limit consistent enterprise rollout.
Availability does not establish adoption, blocked incidents, reduced loss, or operational maturity.
stories.analysis: The agent endpoint is becoming an ordinary security asset: discover it, name it, assign an owner, inspect its protocol, and watch its traffic. That is overdue. The firewall can reject a malformed message; it still cannot tell whether a perfectly formed request should have been allowed to move money or touch production.

stories.title: The safety limit moved upstream.
stories.summary: OpenAI disclosed internal pretraining-loss measurements and proposed using comparable upstream metrics to pace frontier development against monitoring milestones. The signal is a governance proposal—not a universal intelligence score, causal risk threshold, adopted standard, or independently reproduced result.
stories.topic: Upstream capability metrics and frontier-development pacing
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: A frontier lab watches a held-out pretraining metric before the model reaches a familiar benchmark or deployment gate. Crossing a pre-registered threshold does not prove a capability, but it pauses further scaling until an agreed monitoring or interpretability milestone is ready and independently checked.

facts.text: OpenAI published Perplexity and Intelligence on 22 November 2026 and reported approximate log-perplexity values measured on a fixed snapshot of an internal code dataset.

OpenAI reports approximately 0.99 for GPT-3.5, 0.91 for GPT-4, values below 0.8 for newer systems it associates with stronger cybersecurity and mathematics capability, and about 0.76 for a model it says began producing groundbreaking mathematical results.
The article proposes that frontier developers establish shared norms for comparing pretraining loss and consider development limits tied to monitoring or interpretability milestones.
OpenAI's suggested shared limit is a proposal rather than a current rule or adopted cross-lab standard.

OpenAI forecasts that further transformative capabilities could emerge around a 0.68 to 0.7 log-perplexity range; the article presents this as an extrapolation, not an observed result or release roadmap.

OpenAI states that dataset choice complicates cross-lab comparison, loss does not directly correspond to an actionable task, post-training methods can add capability without reducing pretraining loss, and the theoretical loss floor is unknown.
The article does not publish the held-out dataset, evaluation code, exact model-by-model measurements, uncertainty intervals, run variance, contamination analysis, or external audit.

stories.changed: A frontier laboratory has made an upstream training metric part of public governance discussion and attached a concrete pacing idea to it. The new artifact is not a verified capability threshold. It is a proposal to define a limit before downstream evaluations fully reveal what a model can do.
stories.whyItMatters: Capability benchmarks change, saturate, and often describe risk after training has already produced it. A comparable upstream measure could create earlier warning and a decision point—if laboratories publish compatible evaluations, pre-register triggers, and bind those triggers to auditable consequences rather than treating the metric as explanatory branding.
stories.technicalImpact: Treat pretraining loss as one monitoring input, not a general-intelligence score. Fix and document evaluation datasets, separate pretraining from post-training and inference-time gains, report uncertainty and run variance, test for contamination, preserve downstream task evaluations, and define the exact operational action attached to each threshold.
stories.businessImpact: Boards, regulators, and frontier-lab risk teams may gain an earlier planning signal for monitoring investment and deployment gates. A private, lab-specific metric can also create false precision, competitive disclosure risk, and governance theater if other developers cannot reproduce it or if crossing a line has no enforceable consequence.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if several laboratories publish comparable held-out evaluations, pre-register thresholds, and connect them to enforceable monitoring or interpretability milestones, upstream loss could become one input to frontier pacing. If datasets remain private and incomparable, it will remain an internal progress measure presented as a shared standard.
uncertainties: All measurements, historical associations, and forecasts are reported by OpenAI and have not been independently reproduced on the unpublished internal dataset.
The disclosed values are approximate and lack uncertainty intervals, run variance, exact model-by-model tables, contamination analysis, and external audit.
Correlation between lower loss and selected historical capabilities does not establish a causal threshold for any future capability or risk.
Tools, scaffolding, post-training, inference-time reasoning, and deployment context can materially change capability without a corresponding change in this pretraining metric.
Different laboratories use different datasets and mixtures, limiting direct cross-lab comparison unless they agree on a common evaluation protocol.
The proposed pacing limit is not an adopted OpenAI policy, cross-lab agreement, regulatory rule, or enforceable standard in the reviewed source.
The 0.68 to 0.7 range is an extrapolated forecast rather than an observed capability transition or release plan.
stories.analysis: A number becomes governance only when crossing it changes what happens next. OpenAI has supplied an unusual upstream measurement and a proposal for a brake. The hard work begins where the chart ends: comparable data, independent scrutiny, a pre-registered trigger, and consequences that survive competitive pressure.
stories.sourceNote: OpenAI is both the source of the internal measurements and the author of the interpretation, forecast, and pacing proposal. This story keeps those four layers separate and does not treat the private dataset, approximate historical relationship, forecast range, or proposed limit as independently validated or adopted.

review.notes: The OpenAI article's approximate internal measurements, dataset description, stated limitations, forecast language, and shared-pacing proposal were checked. Copy separates measurement, interpretation, extrapolation, and proposal and avoids presenting perplexity as a universal intelligence score or adopted safety threshold.
